# Discovery

Build a complete inventory of source pages before writing any MDX. Most migration gaps come from pages nobody found.

## Get the source

There are three ways in. Prefer them in this order: repo, export, live site. If it is unclear which the user has, ask. Each source guide (`mint migrate --from <name>`) lists that platform's specifics under the same three headings.

**Source of truth.** With the platform's source (a repo, or an export that includes its config and nav files), the code is the source of truth: navigation, labels, order, nesting, tabs, URLs and the OpenAPI spec are exactly what it declares. Use the live site only to fill gaps the code does not cover. Only when scraping (the live-site route, or an export without nav data) do you reconstruct structure, and only then does cleanup judgment apply.

Wherever the source comes from, never modify or delete it. Write the Mintlify project to a separate directory: ask the user where if it is not obvious, otherwise create a new folder. Never overwrite existing content.

### From the repo

- Docs are often a subfolder of a larger product repo or monorepo. Find the docs root and the platform config before inventorying.
- Convert from the repo files directly; the `mirror/` download step does not apply.
- If the repo builds, build the old site once with the tool and plugins its CI pins, into a folder outside both projects. Its output is the old URL list (`sitemap.xml` or the emitted `.html` files) and the record of what includes, macros and plugins actually rendered. Convert from source; check output against the build.
- If the user wants the Mintlify project inside the source repo instead, add the platform's config, theme source, `node_modules/` and build output to `.mintignore`. Mintlify loads every `.js` and `.css` file in the content directory on every page.

Reference: https://www.mintlify.com/docs/organize/mintignore.md

### From an export

- Unzip each export into its own folder and treat it as read-only source, like a repo.
- Inspect its layout (folder structure and a few files of each type) before assuming one. Layouts vary by platform, editor and version.
- An export covers only what its options and the exporting user's access included. Reconcile it against the live site's page list and report anything missing.

### From the live site

Mirror the raw source (below), then convert from the mirror. Find pages with:

- **Sitemap.** Fetch `/sitemap.xml`. If the root element is `<sitemapindex>`, fetch every child `<sitemap><loc>` and merge their `<url><loc>` entries, recursing through nested indexes. The index itself is not the URL list.
- **Machine-readable indexes.** `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, search index JSON, route manifests, framework payloads.
- **Raw endpoints.** `<url>.md` or a JSON content payload per page, where the platform serves one. Rendered HTML only as a fallback.

## Find every page

Combine every source the route offers, then dedupe:

- **Navigation.** Header tabs, every sidebar (each tab can have its own), footer links, "next/previous" and related-page links.
- **In-page links.** Follow internal docs links recursively. Stop only after two consecutive passes find zero new in-scope pages.
- **Variants.** Versions and languages, if present. Ask the user which versions and languages to migrate; record the rest as `excluded` with a reason.

For a repo or export, the file tree plus the platform's nav config (sidebar file, `SUMMARY.md`, `mkdocs.yml` and so on) is the inventory. Still check for pages the config references but the tree lacks, and files the config never references.

Normalize every URL: drop `#fragments`, pick one trailing-slash form and use it everywhere, and dedupe query-only variants unless they serve different content.

## Manifest

Keep `migration-manifest.json` at the root of the Mintlify project, one entry per discovered page:

```json
{
  "source_url": "https://docs.example.com/guides/setup",
  "source_title": "Setting up your workspace",
  "source_sidebar_label": "Setup",
  "nav_section": "Guides > Getting started",
  "converted_file": "guides/setup.mdx",
  "status": "todo",
  "notes": ""
}
```

`status` is one of `todo`, `done`, `excluded`, `blocked`. `excluded` and `blocked` need a concrete reason in `notes`; `blocked` also needs the next step (for example "private section; needs an export that includes it").

If the source links pages by id or title, record each page's id and title here too; link rewriting needs them (`mint migrate --topic conversion`, Links).

## Mirror the raw source

Live-site route only. Download every page into `mirror/`, one file per URL, before converting. Prefer the most structured endpoint the platform offers: raw markdown, a JSON content payload, then rendered HTML. Add `mirror/`, transformer scripts and the manifest to `.mintignore`.

Fetch in parallel for large sites:

```bash
xargs -P 20 -I {} sh -c 'curl -sSL --max-time 30 -o "mirror/$(echo {} | sed "s#https://docs.example.com/##; s#/#__#g").md" "{}.md"' < urls.txt
```

Validate the mirror before converting:

- A file starting with `<!DOCTYPE html>` or `<html` is a failed fetch: the endpoint served rendered HTML. Try another endpoint or scrape that page.
- Site and section roots do not always answer on `<root>.md` the way leaf pages do. Spot-check each with `curl -sS <url>.md | head -3`; the source guide names the working pattern.
- Platform `.md` endpoints add text that is not page content: a header line or block, generated frontmatter, and footer sections. The source guide lists them. Strip them before converting.

## Missing pages

When a URL fails, tell two cases apart:

- **Wrong endpoint.** The page exists but the raw endpoint does not resolve for it. Try the alternatives above, then the rendered page.
- **Stale sitemap entry.** The URL 404s on every endpoint, including the rendered page. Sitemaps often keep removed pages. Mark it `excluded` with `notes: "404 on all endpoints"` and leave it out of navigation.

## Gated content

If pages sit behind a login, paywall or private visibility, do not guess their content and never ask for credentials. Mark them `blocked` and ask the user for an export that includes them.
